A beacon the enemy could use too likely

The property that brought Allen’s aircraft home was the same one that worried the Navy. A broadcast station is a free beacon for anyone with a loop aerial, and Australian authorities acted on it: 4KA at Ayr, on the coast some fifty miles south-east of Townsville, was banned by the Navy from broadcasting at night from 3 March 1942 to 12 April 1943, on the grounds that its signal could be used as a homing device by enemy bombers. Allen’s flight was a daylight one — he describes a clear run over the Coral Sea before the storm forced them down to the waves — so a north Queensland station would have been on the air for him. Whether 4TO itself came under the same night restriction is not recorded in the sources consulted here. The detail is worth keeping anyway, because it shows how thin the line was between navigation aid and liability in 1942.

Sources: Australian Radio History: Qld AM Stations — Wikibooks (4KA Ayr banned by the Navy from night broadcasts 3 Mar 1942 — 12 Apr 1943 as a possible homing device); Queensland A.M. Radio Stations (Australian AM Radio History).

Homing on Townsville likely

The radio compass on that flight deck was almost certainly the SCR-269, standardised in January 1940: a BC-433 receiver, a rotatable loop aerial, a BC-434 control box and an I-81 or I-82 needle indicator, tuning 200 to 1,750 kilocycles, a range that swallows the whole commercial broadcast band. Tune it to a strong station and the needle points at the transmitter, which is precisely the procedure Allen describes to the co-pilot. The station is harder to pin down than the method.

Townsville’s commercial station was 4TO, opened by AWA on 5 October 1931 — the mayor at the microphone, two hundred local artists in the Theatre Royal — running only about 200 watts through the war years and not raised to 500 until 1948; a Townsville broadcast year book for 1946-47 records it at 384 metres, 780 kilocycles. The ABC’s 4QN, opened 26 November 1936, also served the town. No Townsville broadcaster has been found on 610 kilocycles, and Allen himself hedged the figure sixty-odd years after the fact; the number is uncertain, the technique is not.

Sources: Radio Compass SCR-269 (BC-433 receiver, LP-21 loop, I-81/I-82 indicators, 200–1750 kc) — Radiomuseum; SCR-269 — RadioNerds; 4TO Townsville, North Queensland — Radio Heritage Foundation (“384 Metres 780 K/C’s”); Australian Radio History: Qld AM Stations — Wikibooks (4TO opened 5 Oct 1931 on 200 watts, 500 watts in 1948; 4QN opened 26 Nov 1936).

So I said, go up there and just make a tap, and we'll see what, just enough that we can have radio signals here between the base and planes on the field. Just to check out the radios. Well, would you know that, that worked like under the tree, because it worked good, and I could work the planes on the other side of New Guinea or across the mountain. And we were the only squadron that could. And we were the only squadron that could do it. And then the one day, they'd come around, they'd inspect your, and he says, oh, it's no good. He said, you have to tear that down, he said, and put it up according to the book. And our officer says, you don't get anywhere near that. We're the only squadron in the group that can work the planes on the other side of the mountain. Hands off. So why it worked as well as it did, I don't know. Because it was against all the rules. It was against all the rules of whatever. Yeah, too bad. Yeah. Living conditions. Natives.

“Revent” Was a Revetment

One word in the transcript looks like machine-transcription noise and is in fact a precise piece of airfield vocabulary. Allen describes “a different place, cut out, called Revent, where you parked the planes.” He is saying revetment — an earth-walled bay, bulldozed or dug out well away from the runway, into which a single aircraft was taxied so that a bomb falling on one machine would not take the whole squadron with it.

The record for 17-Mile describes exactly this: dispersal and camp areas southeast of the runway, with revetments carved into the hillsides and the taxiways raised so they would drain. At 7-Mile the Americans began building them in earnest right after the heavy Japanese raid of 17 August 1942, and a few of those bomber revetments survived at Jacksons airport into this century. Sixty-odd years on, Allen was still reaching for the right technical term for a hole in a Papuan hillside.

Sources: Pacific Wrecks — 17 Mile Drome (Durand, Waigani); Pacific Wrecks — 7 Mile Drome (Jackson Airport).

The crocodile above the pool

Three crocodiles are now recognised on New Guinea. The saltwater or estuarine crocodile, Crocodylus porosus, is the largest living reptile, with the largest reliably measured animal at a total length of at least 615 centimetres, and it ranges from southwestern India and Sri Lanka through southeast Asia and the Indonesian archipelago to the Solomons; it tolerates everything from fresh water to full-strength sea water and moves well up rivers and into swamps and lagoons.

The New Guinea crocodile, Crocodylus novaeguineae, is a smaller freshwater animal, the males reaching about three and a half metres, living in the swamps, marshes and lakes of the northern half of the island; a third, Hall’s New Guinea crocodile, was separated from it in 2019 and belongs to the country south of the central ranges. Allen’s squadron was on the northern side, which leaves the saltwater crocodile and the New Guinea crocodile as the candidates, and the record does not settle which one it was. The explanation he was given, that the carcass would be left to lie until the evil spirits were out of it before it was butchered, came from an Australian standing beside him rather than from the men who had killed it, and it is best read as one European’s gloss on a practice he had watched, not as any Papuan’s account of his own belief.

Sources: Estuarine Crocodile, The Australian Museum; New Guinea crocodile (Crocodylus novaeguineae); Saltwater Crocodile, Queensland Museum Collections; Hall’s New Guinea crocodile (Crocodylus halli), described 2019.

Why the villages were so quiet

Allen noticed that the people kept their distance and that he saw few of them, and there is a documented reason beyond shyness. From 21 March 1942 the Australian New Guinea Administrative Unit, ANGAU, governed civil affairs in both Papua and the Mandated Territory, and its largest single task was raising and directing indigenous labour for the Australian and American forces. At its September 1944 peak more than thirty-five thousand men were involved in the organisation, directed by some two thousand Australian officers, first carrying and portering, later building; the airstrips, roads and supply dumps the Americans used were in substantial part their work.

Recruitment was not voluntary: an order of June 1942 let ANGAU contract Papuans for up to three years and forbade them to desert or refuse work, and the carrier rolls went from about two thousand that month to over sixteen thousand by December. The cost is on the record: at least 2,024 ANGAU carriers and labourers died during the war, mainly of infectious disease such as malaria and dysentery, with 46 killed by enemy action and 91 wounded. A village whose fit men were away under indenture would look to a passing airman much as Allen describes it. This is a group-level fact about the Territory rather than a finding about the particular hamlets he walked into, which the record does not identify.

Sources: Casualties in Australian Military and Indigenous Para-Military Units in Papua New Guinea during the Second World War, Journal of Military and Veterans’ Health; Australian New Guinea Administrative Unit; The Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels: looking beyond the myth, Australian War Memorial.

The bag, and the man with the stick likely

What Allen saw tied over the woman’s forehead was a bilum, the looped string bag of New Guinea, made by hand from spun plant fibre in a technique passed down between generations. Its band goes across the forehead so that the bag rides on the back and the carrier’s hands stay free, and the bag stretches to hold whatever is put into it; the Museum of New Zealand’s catalogue note on one collected example says bilums are used by men and women to carry yams, taro and other foodstuffs, and sometimes even babies. That also answers the thing which puzzled him, that he could see no gardens near the hamlets, because the garden produce he did not see was moving past him inside the bag he did see.

The division of carrying he read as a man doing nothing had been read the same way by outsiders before him, among them Matthew Stirling, on the 1926 Dutch and American expedition to Dutch New Guinea, who wrote on 7 May that year, at Soeroei on Japen, that the women invariably carried all the load while the men walked alongside quite unburdened — though that was an island a thousand miles west of Allen’s coast and other people entirely. What the arrangement meant to the families walking that track is not something a young American passing on a road could establish, and the record does not settle it. What can be said is that the bilum itself was a valued made thing, and not merely a load.

What the briefings told them: 32 to 34 years, and do not go west likely

Two things Allen carried away from his briefings are worth unpicking. A life expectancy of 32 to 34 years is a period life-table figure, an average across everyone born, and in a population with heavy infant and child mortality it is dragged down hard by deaths in the first few years; it never meant that the adults in front of him would be dead at 33, and populations with such figures routinely contain old people. No census had counted most of the interior in 1943, so any number handed to American troops was an estimate rather than a measurement.

The rule against going west rested less on a proven belt of headhunters than on the limits of the colonial administration itself: the country beyond the patrol posts was, in the administration’s own language, uncontrolled, and the last of the great exploring patrols into it, led by the patrol officer Jim Taylor with John Black, came out of the country between Mount Hagen and the Sepik in 1939, only a few years before Allen reached New Guinea — a journey the historian Bill Gammage reconstructed in The Sky Travellers. Headhunting is documented for particular peoples in particular places, but the blanket claim he was given was a colonial commonplace rather than a description of the country a day’s walk inland from his strip. The order also made plain military sense, because west and north-west was where the Japanese were. His words here come through the transcript garbled, and are given as recorded.

Sources: Life expectancy: how is it calculated and how should it be interpreted? Our World in Data; Papua New Guinea population and demography country profile, Our World in Data; Jim Taylor (explorer), on the 1938-39 Hagen-Sepik Patrol with John Black; The Sky Travellers: Journeys in New Guinea 1938–1939, Bill Gammage (1998).

The missionaries, and what had happened at Dobodura likely

When Allen said the people along that coast had been in contact with the missionaries, he was describing a ruin rather than an institution. The Anglican mission of the Territory of Papua held stations on the north coast at Gona and inland at Sangara and Isivita, in Orokaiva country, and the Japanese came ashore at Gona on 21 July 1942. In the months that followed the Gona party of a priest, a nursing sister and a teacher was broken up, and the two women were killed on Buna beach; the Sangara and Isivita party of two priests, a layman, a nurse and a teacher was taken by villagers and handed over to the Japanese at Dobodura, whence they were taken to Buna and killed.

Dobodura is the plain the Americans then turned into a complex of fifteen landing grounds, and where Allen’s squadron moved on 21 May 1943, nine months after that handover. Churches commemorate 333 church workers of all denominations, Papuan and foreign, killed in New Guinea in 1942 and 1943, on 2 September. That villagers did the handing over belongs in the account as well, and it cannot be read simply as treachery, because the Orokaiva were caught between two armies in their own gardens and had reasons of their own which the mission’s wartime publications were in no position to weigh.

Sources: South Sea Epic, compiled by Ruth Henrich (1944), Project Canterbury / Anglican History; Martyrs of New Guinea; Among the Ruins: The Story of the New Guinea Martyrs, Arthur Bell (1946), Project Canterbury; Dobodura Airfield Complex (1942).

Which pidgin he was hearing

Allen remembered the contact language on the coast as Pidgin English, and in one sense he was right, in that the Americans were meeting a trade language rather than a village one. But the language that carried across the Territory of Papua, where he spent 1943 at Port Moresby and Dobodura, was not Tok Pisin. It was Police Motu, a simplified form of the Motu language of the Port Moresby coast, which spread with the Papuan constabulary — hence the name — and became the administration’s working tongue through Papua, and which was officially renamed Hiri Motu in the early 1970s, on the reasoning that the language’s history was older than the name Police Motu implied.

Tok Pisin, the English-vocabulary pidgin that Americans usually meant by the phrase, had grown out of the Pacific labour trade and the plantations of the Bismarck Archipelago, and spread through the former German territory in the north; its expansion south into Papua was, in one survey’s words, much more restricted until recent years. Allen would have come within its range only in February 1944, at Nadzab in the Markham valley. The likeliest reading is that Pidgin English was his catch-all for whatever contact speech he heard, which is what the phrase generally meant in an American’s mouth in 1943.

Sources: Tok Pisin survey chapter, APiCS Online (Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures); Hiri Motu (Police Motu); Hiri Motu, Encyclopaedia Britannica; 90th Attack Squadron (formerly 90th Bombardment Squadron) — WWII stations list.

The switchboard with the little flappers

The board Allen calls an antique was almost certainly one of the Signal Corps’ local-battery field switchboards, the six-line BD-71 or its twelve-line twin, the BD-72. Each line carried a hinged shutter, a “drop”, released by the ringing current when a subscriber wound the hand crank on his telephone, so the shutter fell open and showed the operator which line was calling; a night alarm buzzed until it was reset. The operator listened on a chest set, plugged a cord into the called party’s jack and turned the board’s own magneto crank, about a hundred volts, to ring the bell at the far end.

The instruments on the other ends of those lines were EE-8 field telephones, adopted in 1935, powered by dry cells with a hand-cranked generator for signalling and good for something like seven miles of field wire. Allen was right about the design if not the date: cord-and-drop switchboards were a nineteenth-century idea still standard issue in 1942, because they needed nothing but batteries, wire and a man’s arm. The wire was the other half of the job, and the hard half — he remembers baked Australian ground that had to be dug or the line swung up through trees to cross a dirt road, and lines kept off the mud in New Guinea.

Sources: Field Telephones, BD-71 Switchboard and Residential Crank Phones (operation of the drops, magneto ringing, BD-72 as the 12-line version); BD-71 Field Switch Board and EE-8B Field Telephones — USRadioguy; TM 11-330, Switchboards BD-71, BD-72 (War Department Technical Manual, 1 Dec 1944); The EE-8 Field Telephone — The National WWII Museum.

Guinea Gold

New Guinea was the only WW2 theater where U.S. troops relied on a locally produced paper instead of Stars and Stripes. Guinea Gold began daily publication 19 November 1942 in Port Moresby, ran continuously for 1,320 days, and carried General MacArthur's communiqués 20 hours ahead of the rest of the world's press. At its peak it reached roughly 37,000 U.S. troops daily. The family holds an original February 1944 issue.

Source: Australian War Memorial.

Where The Warning Came From

The alert that emptied Allen’s part of the strip came out of one of the more remarkable improvisations of the Papuan campaign. In January 1942 Major Donald Small, chief signals officer of the 8th Military District, threw a ring of wireless observation posts around Port Moresby at a radius of roughly 150 kilometres; the New Guinea Air Warning Wireless, known to everyone as the Spotters, grew from sixteen stations to sixty-one with 180 men by the end of 1942, and to more than 150 posts by late 1944, absorbing Army, RAAF and civilian coastwatcher stations under one command from October 1942. Two rings did the work.

The outer gave about an hour’s notice; the inner ring, at some fifty kilometres, gave ten minutes. Radar helped too, and on 12 April 1943 the incoming formation was tracked by the set atop Paga Hill as it crossed the range. That arithmetic is exactly the experience Allen describes: against high-flying aircraft coming over the mountains the warning arrived measured in minutes, and a formation at 25,000 feet could be directly overhead before anyone on the field had looked up.

Sources: New Guinea Air Warning Wireless (Wikipedia); Pacific Wrecks — Operation I-Go: April 12, 1943 (radar atop Paga Hill); Battle of Port Moresby — Virtual Remembrance Trail (Australian Government).

The Raid That Went Over Their Heads likely

Allen gives no date, and the transcript cannot supply one. But the numbers he remembers narrow the field sharply. The 3rd Bomb Group was based at Port Moresby from 28 January to 20 May 1943, and in that window only one Japanese raid came anywhere near a hundred aircraft: the strike of 12 April 1943, flown as part of Admiral Yamamoto’s Operation I-Go. Pacific Wrecks counts roughly 175 machines; the bomber force was some 43 or 44 G4M Bettys and the escort at least 131 Zeros, with the sources differing on the exact split.

It is recorded as the largest force ever sent against Port Moresby; it climbed in tight V formations and bombed from about 25,000 feet between 10.15 and 10.25 in the morning. Five strips were bombed and only four are named in the record: 5-Mile (Wards), 3-Mile (Kila Kila), 12-Mile (Berry) and 14-Mile (Schwimmer). Allen’s own 17-Mile Durand is not among those four, though the unnamed fifth leaves real room for doubt, and 12-Mile and 14-Mile are the two strips nearest his. The match is close enough to be worth saying out loud and loose enough that it must be offered as the likeliest candidate rather than a certainty.

Sources: Pacific Wrecks — Operation I-Go: April 12, 1943, last major Japanese air raid over Port Moresby; Pacific Wrecks — Japanese air raids and missions against Port Moresby; 3rd Bombardment Group — base list with dates (historyofwar.org); Operation I-Go (Wikipedia).

The Tent With the Unsealed Envelope

The procedure Allen describes was the Army’s standard method, and the unsealed envelope was the whole point of it. A soldier overseas was forbidden to use a civilian mailbox; War Department Pamphlet 21-1, issued 29 July 1943, told him under the heading “Enlisted Men” to “Place your letter unsealed in your organization mail box, never in any civil post office box,” and reminded him, “You are required to use the Army Postal Service, and the Army Postal Service only.” A censor officer of his own organization read it before it travelled on, and the Army required mail to be “completely through censorship within 48 hours.” The signature he may have seen belonged to the officers’ rule alongside his own: an officer censored his own letter, sealed it, and signed the lower left-hand corner, his mail still “subject to further censorship examination by base censorship detachments.” Ten “don’ts” were set before him.

Eight were subjects — the location, strength, materiel and equipment of Army units, military installations, transportation facilities, convoys with their routes, ports and time en route, movements of ships, troops and aircraft, plans and forecasts for future operations, the effects of enemy operations, and casualties before official release — and two were habits: no code or cipher, and no disclosing his location except as authorized. The envelope was policed as tightly as the letter, since “No geographical location of sender may be shown on an envelope or other outside cover” — which is why an APO number, and not a place, was all his family ever saw. The officer who did the reading in the 90th Bomb Squadron has not been identified from the surviving records.

Sources: Secrecy in Wartime: U.S. War Department Pamphlet No. 21-1, “When You Are Overseas These Facts are Vital” (29 July 1943); Mail Call: V-mail, The National WWII Museum; Safeguarding Military Information, Army Regulations No. 380-5, 28 September 1942 (archival record).

Why Nobody Turned On A Light likely

Allen supplies his own explanation, and it is the one the record supports. A single aircraft circling in the dark did little harm by itself; its real work was to scout, to keep men out of their cots, and, when it carried flares, to mark for someone else. On the night of 13-14 October 1942 at Henderson Field the battleships Kongo and Haruna opened fire at 01:33 and shelled the Lunga perimeter for 83 minutes with more than 900 fourteen-inch rounds, destroying 48 of the 90 aircraft on the field, burning nearly all the aviation fuel and killing forty-one men.

Set against a risk like that, a searchlight beam and a stream of tracer amounted to a free fix on the runway and on the gun pits themselves. The contrast with daylight is stark: during the 12 April 1943 raid the Australian anti-aircraft batteries around Port Moresby fired 1,112 rounds and claimed no hits at all. By day there was nothing left to conceal; by night there was everything.

Sources: Washing Machine Charlie (Wikipedia) — purposes including flare-dropping for naval and ground forces; Henderson Field (Guadalcanal) (Wikipedia); Battle for Henderson Field (Wikipedia) — 13-14 October 1942 battleship bombardment; Pacific Wrecks — Operation I-Go: April 12, 1943 (1,112 AA rounds, no hits claimed).

The Joker Who Circled: Washing Machine Charlie

Allen never gives the aeroplane a name; he calls it the joker. Allied troops across the Pacific had a name for it, and it came from the sound. A pilot flying a twin-engined machine could throw his engines out of synchronisation to produce a slow, uneven throb, loud enough to wake a camp and then keep it awake, and so the lone nightly visitor became Washing Machine Charlie; the comparison to a pre-war Maytag is often repeated but we could not source it.

The types varied, from ship- and shore-based single-engined seaplanes of the R-Area Air Force to Mitsubishi G4M Betty bombers flown deliberately out of step, and the jobs varied with them: scouting, dropping flares for Japanese naval or ground forces, bombing airfields and installations, and simply keeping a whole base awake and braced. A companion nickname, Bedcheck Charlie, belonged chiefly to the lone Luftwaffe visitors over Europe but reached the Pacific too, in an Associated Press despatch from the Gilberts dated 12 January 1944. The names are best documented at Henderson Field and across the Solomons and travelled to other Allied bases; nothing in Allen’s account shows the 90th Bomb Squadron used them, so the nickname belongs on the page as context rather than as his word.

Sources: Washing Machine Charlie (Wikipedia); Charlie — Wordorigins.org (earliest ‘Bedcheck Charley’ citation, AP, 12 January 1944); Henderson Field (Guadalcanal) (Wikipedia) — checked, contains no mention of Louie the Louse or Washing Machine Charlie.

V-Mail

The censorship Allen describes — envelopes left unsealed for an officer to read before sending — was standard practice; V-Mail (Victory Mail) was the answer to what came next. A letter written on special stationery was censored, then photographed onto microfilm, shipped home at a fraction of the bulk of the original paper, and printed back out at about one-quarter size for delivery. A letter on microfilm took roughly 1/37th the cargo space of the same letter on paper; over a billion V-Mails were sent between June 1942 and November 1945.

Source: National Postal Museum; The National WWII Museum.

APO 1106 — The Number That Isn’t There

Seven of Allen’s eight numbers decode. The first one does not, and the reason is worth recording precisely rather than guessing around. The Army Postal Service’s own master register of every APO used between January 1942 and November 1947 runs 1102, 1103, 1105, then jumps to 1112: there is no APO 1106 in it at all, and the surrounding 1100-series numbers were routed through New York and opened in 1945 and 1946 for occupied Europe, not the Pacific. The San Francisco-routed numbers above 1000 were assigned to the Philippines and the Ryukyus in 1945, after Allen was already home. So 1106 cannot be a place he served under, and the honest conclusion is that this figure is either something other than an APO — a unit number, a shipment or class number, a date — or a slip of the pen or of the copying. The page in the book is worth looking at again with fresh eyes.

Sources: Numerical Listing of APO’s, January 1942 — November 1947 (AGO), p. 198 — the sequence runs 1102 (Le Mans), 1103 (Tannenberg/Marburg), 1105 (France, then Manila), 1112 (Berlin); no 1106 is listed; WWII Army Post Office (APO) Locations — database transcribed from the 1949 AGO listing; no entry for APO 1106; APO-locations.csv — full 1100-series enumeration confirming no APO 1106 and New York routing throughout.

APO 501 — The Theatre Address likely

APO 501 was the theatre headquarters post office for United States Army forces in the Southwest Pacific, and the Army’s own register tracks its moves well to the rear of the fighting: Melbourne from January 1942, Sydney from September 1942, Brisbane from February 1943, then forward to Hollandia on 25 November 1944, Tacloban on Leyte on 5 February 1945, and Manila on 7 March 1945, closing on 5 May 1946. Allen landed at Brisbane on 25 February 1942, in the weeks when 501 was still physically at Melbourne — which is the point of the number rather than a contradiction of it.

A theatre-level APO was an address, not a place; it was what a man newly arrived in Australia and not yet on any base-section roll could give his family. That 501 heads the Australian part of his list, ahead of the local Queensland numbers, fits that reading, though nothing in the record states which address his first letters home actually carried.

Sources: Numerical Listing of APO’s, January 1942 — November 1947 (AGO), p. 121 — APO 501: Melbourne 1/42, Sydney 9/42, Brisbane 2/43, Hollandia 25-11-44, Tacloban 5-2-45, Manila 7-3-45; Army Post Offices in Australia during WW2, Peter Dunn’s Australia @ War; Army Post Offices in Australia during WW2 — APO 501 listed as “Hqs. U.S. Army Forces Far East” (no dates given).

The news before the movie

The two voices Allen names were the two that carried to the Southwest Pacific. KGEI was built by General Electric for the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island in 1939, and moved in 1941 to the Redwood Peninsula three miles east of Belmont, California — a 50-kilowatt transmitter behind three-foot concrete walls, floors and ceilings. For a time it was, in its own historians’ words, the only station on which news from the United States could be heard in the Pacific.

From London, the BBC’s Overseas Service ran a dedicated Pacific Service, and by the end of December 1941 the Corporation’s three daily services to the Pacific, the East and Africa, together with the nightly service to Canada and the United States, totalled over twenty-one hours out of every twenty-four. What makes Allen’s bulletin board remarkable is the date. Organised forces broadcasting only reached New Guinea in 1944 — the station at Milne Bay on 26 January, 9PA at Port Moresby opened by General MacArthur on 26 February, the AFRS Jungle Network headquartered at Hollandia — so for a year and more the only news a squadron got was whatever a radio man could tune, write down fast and read out loud. The neighbouring squadron running a line over to hear it was not a small courtesy; it was the local news service.

Sources: KGEI History — The Radio Historian; KGEI — Wikipedia; BBC Year Book 1942 (three daily services to the Pacific, the East and Africa; over 21 hours out of 24); AFRS Jungle Network — Radio Heritage Foundation.

Christmas in the Southwest Pacific, and Somewhere to Go

The services worked hard to mark the day at the far end of the supply line. The Army Postal Service told families to mail Christmas parcels for men overseas between 15 September and 15 October, months ahead, and the mail itself came in two forms: ordinary letters, which the men much preferred — Navy personnel in 1944 got about six of them for every V-mail — and V-mail, the photographed and shrunken letter written on a single sheet that folded into its own envelope, of which more than a billion were processed between June 1942 and November 1945. Either way it came in surges, which is why Allen remembers weeks of nothing and then a whole bundle at once.

Turkey dinners were pushed forward wherever the logistics reached, and across the theater men improvised the day out of what was at hand. And there were the pictures. The Army’s motion picture service ran 260 film libraries feeding sixty bases on six continents, moving reels by boat, plane, train, automobile, motorcycle, camel caravan and Arctic dog sled, and in the South Pacific the men built their own theaters — benches cut from palm trunks and a white sheet hung from the branches. That is the theater Allen was headed to with a scorpion on his hand, and the one where, by his own account, he used to plug in his shortwave set and read the day’s news aloud before the show started, until another squadron ran a line up to his tent to hear it too.

Sources: How the U.S. Army Served its Movie-Mad GIs during World War II — National Archives, The Unwritten Record; Mail Call: V-mail — The National WWII Museum; Wrap Securely, Address Correctly: Innovations of Postal Mail during World War II — Kentucky Historical Society; Christmas for Australians away from home during World War II — Anzac Portal, DVA.

The Scorpion in the Barracks Bag

Of roughly 2,770 described scorpion species, only about 104 — 3.8 percent, and almost all of them in the family Buthidae — are considered medically significant, and the dangerous ones are concentrated far from New Guinea: Androctonus, Buthus and Leiurus across North Africa, the Middle East and Asia, Tityus in South America and the Caribbean, Centruroides in Mexico, Central America and the American southwest, with Mexico, Brazil, Iran, Algeria and Morocco carrying the deaths. No Australasian region appears on that list. New Guinea’s own scorpions are a smaller cast — four genera in two families, the hormurids Hormurus and Liocheles alongside the buthids Isometrus and Lychas.

The Australian Museum, describing the twenty-nine species in six genera found across Australia, puts the likely outcome plainly: they can give a painful sting causing inflammation and pain for several hours, treated with a cold pack and a doctor if the pain persists. What the medics at Dobodura had to offer was therefore symptomatic — and for any puncture of the skin, a needle. The Army had been immunizing every soldier with tetanus toxoid since 1941, boosting with toxoid rather than horse serum at the time of a wound, a regime so effective that the whole Army recorded just twelve cases of tetanus in the war, one per million soldiers, and most of those twelve had not been fully immunized. Allen’s shot was most plausibly that, or morphine for the pain; the record does not settle which, and the honest reading of the episode is that he was in real pain, in no real danger, and back in his seat before the picture finished.

Sources: Scorpionism: a neglected tropical disease with global public health implications — Frontiers in Public Health; Scorpions — Australian Museum; Atlas of Australasian hormurid scorpions I: the genus Hormurus in Papua New Guinea — Revue Suisse de Zoologie; Early U.S. Military Immunization Against Tetanus and Diphtheria: Historical Context and Current Importance.

Which Christmas: Dobodura, 1943

The interview never dates the story, but the group’s own movements narrow it to one night. The 3rd Bombardment Group reached Charters Towers in Queensland on 10 March 1942, moved up to Port Moresby on 28 January 1943, to Dobodura on 20 May 1943, and on to Nadzab on 3 February 1944; Allen went home in the autumn of 1944. That leaves Christmas 1942 spent in the dry savanna country of north Queensland and exactly one Christmas in New Guinea — 25 December 1943, at Dobodura, on the grass flats inland from the northern Papuan coast.

He calls it Christmas in the jungle, and Dobodura is the only Christmas that fits the phrase. It was not a quiet week: the 1st Marine Division went ashore at Cape Gloucester on 26 December 1943, and the group supported those landings, including an attack on Japanese machine-gun positions on 28 December flown by its A-20 squadrons. Whether Allen’s own 90th Bomb Squadron flew on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day itself, the record consulted here does not say.

Sources: 3rd Bombardment Group — historyofwar.org; Dobodura Airfield Complex (1942) — Wikipedia; Neutralisation of Rabaul — Wikipedia.

There Was No Station Yet: How the Music Got In likely

Allen sets the scene simply — two men writing letters with the radio on — but in December 1943 there was still no Allied forces station broadcasting from anywhere in New Guinea for that radio to tune. RAAF Radio Milne Bay, the first of the Jungle Network stations in the islands, did not open until 26 January 1944; the Australian Army’s 9PA at Port Moresby was opened by General MacArthur and the ABC’s Sir Charles Moses on 26 February 1944, and relayed to every ABC station at home; Nadzab followed in June 1944, staffed out of Milne Bay, and Madang in October.

The Armed Forces Radio Service itself had been established by War Department order on 26 May 1942, with headquarters in Los Angeles, and by VJ Day it had pressed its millionth transcription disc; it fed set pieces like the Command Performance Christmas special of 24 December 1942, carried by all four networks, and the ninety-minute 1943 edition. But with no local transmitter in range, what came into that tent almost certainly came the way Allen describes everywhere else in his interview: shortwave, out of KGEI in San Francisco, which had been beaming to American forces in the Pacific since February 1939 and was carrying Command Performance to the South Pacific by mid-1942. The inference about his particular set is ours; the station dates are documented.

Sources: Australian Military WWII Broadcasting Stations; Christmas on the Air — Wartime Radio Programs Revisited — The National WWII Museum; Armed Forces Radio Service — Museum of Broadcast Communications; AFRS Jungle Network — Radio Heritage Foundation.

The Song He Still Cannot Hear Straight Through

Irving Berlin wrote “White Christmas” before the war — by one account in January 1940 — and Bing Crosby gave it its first public airing on his NBC program The Kraft Music Hall in the last days of December 1941, within weeks of Pearl Harbor; sources disagree on whether that broadcast fell on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day, and the point is not settled. Crosby recorded the version America knew on 29 May 1942 at Radio Recorders in Los Angeles, for Decca, with the John Scott Trotter Orchestra and the Ken Darby Singers, in a session that took eighteen minutes. It was released on 30 July 1942 in the six-disc album of 78s from the film Holiday Inn, won Best Original Song at the Academy Awards ceremony held in March 1943, and reached the top of the Billboard chart on 31 October 1942, where it stayed eleven weeks and on into the new year.

Crosby grew wary of singing it for men overseas: he said he hesitated because it invariably caused such a nostalgic yearning among the men that it made them sad — and by his own account they kept asking for it anyway. The pressing Allen would have heard in a tent in New Guinea was that original 1942 master, which Decca wore out from sheer use; Crosby had to re-cut the song on 19 March 1947 to replace it. Seventy years later he told his interviewer he had not heard it once that day without his thoughts going back, which is precisely the effect the singer had been afraid of.

Sources: White Christmas (song) — Wikipedia; Dreaming of a “White Christmas” — The National WWII Museum; The sad story behind ‘White Christmas’ — KUOW; Holiday Inn (film) — Wikipedia.

Bob Hope's “Pineapple Circuit”

In summer 1944 Bob Hope led a USO troupe on a roughly 13,000-mile, 52-day tour of the Pacific, nicknamed the “Pineapple Circuit” — over 80 shows, including a welcome in Sydney on 15 August 1944 and stops at New Guinea-area bases. Its known August 1944 New Guinea/Australia leg matches Allen's account of attending a show.

Source: The National WWII Museum.

Hollandia

From 30 March to 3 April 1944, Fifth Air Force conducted surprise raids on Hollandia's airfields, destroying roughly 400 Japanese aircraft. Ground forces captured the main airfield 22 April 1944 (Operation Reckless); unlike many Japanese strongholds, large numbers of defenders abandoned their positions or surrendered rather than fight to the death — consistent with Allen's account of prisoners taken there.

Source: Wikipedia, Bombing of Hollandia, citing Craven & Cate, USAAF in WWII.

The Prisoners on the Beach

What Allen saw was genuinely unusual. Hollandia was held by about 11,000 Japanese, but only some 500 of them were ground combat troops, drawn from antiaircraft batteries; the rest were service and headquarters personnel of the 6th Air Division of the Fourth Air Army and of the Second Army, and when the landings came at dawn on 22 April they broke and went into the bush, making for Genjem and the long overland route west to Sarmi.

Most Japanese losses at Hollandia therefore came during the weeks of mopping up that followed, with men taken in small groups — starving, sick and cut off. The US Army’s official history records that by 6 June 1944, “611 Japanese were captured and over 3,300 killed.” Its casualty table, whose New Guinea figures run to early October 1944, credits the Hollandia operation with 655 prisoners against 4,475 killed; set beside Aitape’s 100 prisoners taken against 8,825 killed, or Wakde-Sarmi’s 55, that is the largest take of prisoners anywhere in the campaign, with Biak’s 460 the next nearest. Mid-May, when Allen waded ashore, was precisely the season of those round-ups, and a column of prisoners moving along the beach is exactly what the record would predict.

Sources: HyperWar — US Army in WWII: The Approach to the Philippines, ch. III, “The Hollandia Operations” (Robert Ross Smith); HyperWar — The Approach to the Philippines, Appendix: Table 2, Japanese casualties April–December 1944; Battle of Hollandia — garrison composition and withdrawal to Genjem and Sarmi.

Up the Coast by LST

Allen’s account of the move to Hollandia can be dated almost to the day from the official Army Air Forces history, which records that the 3rd Bombardment Group’s waterborne echelon, moving directly from Nadzab via Lae without staging, reached Humboldt Bay between 12 and 15 May 1944. That is his “got on boats up the coast of New Guinea”: down the Markham Valley to Lae, then north-west along the coast and into Humboldt Bay, and off the bow ramps of LSTs into the shallows, which is how ground echelons and their equipment came ashore there. The standard USAAF station list gives the group at Hollandia from 12 May 1944.

One point should be stated plainly rather than smoothed over: the infantry assault had gone in on 22 April, three weeks earlier, not “a day or two before” — sixty years on, the beach was still raw, and the memory has compressed the interval. The aircraft were not waiting for them either. The doldrums had given way to summer drought, and the captured strips were so dusty that on 16 May only one A-20 squadron could be called forward: the 8th, one of the four squadrons of Allen’s own group.

Sources: HyperWar — The Army Air Forces in World War II, Vol. IV, ch. 18 (Craven & Cate, official history); Army Air Corps Museum — 3rd Bombardment Group station list (Hollandia, 12 May 1944); HyperWar — US Army in WWII: The Approach to the Philippines, ch. III (LSTs at Humboldt Bay).

Why the May quarter was still there in September

On 5 April 1944 Fifth Air Force announced that ground personnel who had served “faithfully and continuously overseas for at least eighteen months” might be selected for return to the United States, with preference going to men with six months or more in the islands north of Australia. Allen qualified on both counts and more, but the quotas were minute — about one per cent of the air force’s total ground strength each month.

The entire June-to-August allotment for the 54th Troop Carrier Wing was one officer and five enlisted men. The Army’s own historians calculated that at 1944 rates a complete turnover of Far East Air Forces ground personnel would have taken more than eight years, and the Air Evaluation Board concluded flatly that “the rotation program as executed in the SWPA had a more adverse effect on morale than any other factor.” His one dry sentence about the May quarter still sitting there in September is that policy felt from the inside: his name was on a list, and the list was not moving — which is why the shouting in the camp on his birthday sounded to him at first like a cruel joke.

Sources: Craven & Cate, The Army Air Forces in World War II, Vol. V: The Pacific — Matterhorn to Nagasaki, Chapter 11 (HyperWar).

One ship, no escort likely

Allen’s ship cannot be identified from what he says, and it would be wrong to put a name to it. What he describes, though, is a recognisable type: pre-war passenger liners requisitioned in 1941-42 and run as fast troopships under the War Shipping Administration. Matson Line’s Lurline, Matsonia, Mariposa and Monterey had been built for the Hawaii and Australasia runs out of California, calling at Samoa, Fiji, New Zealand and Australia; all four passed into government hands within weeks of Pearl Harbor — Monterey was handed over at San Francisco on 3 December 1941, four days before the attack — and by Matson’s own reckoning the four made 119 wartime voyages and carried 736,000 troops, a count that comes from the company rather than from a government record.

Because they were fast they frequently ran without a convoy — Monterey “served as a fast troop carrier, often operating alone so she would not be slowed by formation navigation in a convoy” — which is precisely the crossing he remembers, “all by ourselves in one ship,” with everyone aboard letting out a hoot the moment the Golden Gate Bridge passed overhead. One note for the family, offered as a reading and not as evidence: the machine transcript’s nonsense phrase “we had to get for the bats and lions before the war” looks very much like the speech-recogniser mangling “Matson Lines,” which would fit his own description of a California-to-the-Pacific passenger run. Even so, without a sailing list the ship stays unnamed.

Sources: SS Monterey — Wikipedia; SS Lurline (1932) — Wikipedia; Matson — Company History; SS Mariposa (1931) — Wikipedia.

Out of the Jungle: The Markham Valley likely

There is a geographic reason Nadzab felt like relief. The Markham Valley runs roughly 160 kilometres inland from the sea at Lae, climbing about 500 metres along its length, and its floor is a flat expanse of dry kunai grass rather than rainforest — open country, hot and often bone dry, burnt off by local people once a year. Dobodura had been kunai too, but a narrow plain hemmed in by the swamp and bush behind the Buna beaches, and before that came Port Moresby’s dust; Nadzab sat in an open corridor well inland, with the jungle pushed back to the ranges on either side.

Allen’s afternoon change of air is exactly the behaviour such a corridor produces: the valley opens onto the Huon Gulf, and as the inland plain heats through the day it draws air up the valley from the sea. No period meteorological record naming that wind has been found, so the mechanism here is offered as consistent with the geography rather than as documented fact. It is worth noting that other veterans remembered Nadzab as hot, dusty and wet; Allen’s “best place we were at” is a comparison, and the thing he is comparing it to is the jungle.

Sources: Markham Valley — geography, length, elevation and grassland; Pacific Wrecks — Nadzab Airfield (Nadzab No. 1 Strip, East Base), Morobe Province, PNG; Landing at Nadzab — Markham Valley airfield development; Pacific Wrecks — Dobodura Airfield: “the land is mostly kunai”.

Nadzab: The Jump He Arrived After

Nadzab was taken by the first major airborne assault of the Pacific war, on 5 September 1943, months before Allen’s squadron ever saw it. The US Army’s official history records an armada of 302 aircraft drawn from eight different fields: six squadrons of B-25 strafers worked the field over with nose guns and parachute fragmentation bombs, six A-20s laid smoke once the last bomb had gone off, and eighty-one C-47s carrying the 503rd Parachute Infantry Regiment were emptied in four and a half minutes, watched by Generals MacArthur and Kenney from a flight of three B-17s overhead. Australian gunners of the 2/4th Field Regiment jumped with them, and an Australian pioneer battalion that had walked and rafted in began work on the strip the same day.

Within a fortnight the engineers had two parallel 6,000-foot runways down and six more strips started. The 90th Bombardment Squadron flew in from Dobodura on 30 January 1944, with group headquarters following on 3 February — nearly five months after the drop, to a base already largely built. Secondary accounts credit the six smoke-laying A-20s to the 89th Bombardment Squadron, a sister squadron in Allen’s own group, but the official history does not name the unit and that attribution should be treated as unconfirmed.

Sources: HyperWar — US Army in WWII: CARTWHEEL, The Reduction of Rabaul, ch. XI (official history); Landing at Nadzab — forces, casualties and airfield development; Pacific Wrecks — Allied units based at Dobodura Airfield (90th BS departs for Nadzab, 30 Jan 1944); Army Air Corps Museum — 3rd Bombardment Group station list (Nadzab, 3 Feb 1944).

Dobodura: “Below the Bay”

Allen’s “Dogadura” is Dobodura, a plain of kunai grass lying inland from Buna on the north-east coast of Papua rather than the east coast proper. American engineers and infantrymen began clearing there early in November 1942 to support the Buna fighting: a rough strip was usable by 21 November, and three more were finished by 12 December, one with a 4,200-foot runway. The complex kept growing — eleven interconnected strips in the main group, and by Pacific Wrecks’ count fifteen or more runways in the vicinity, many linked by taxiways — until it was one of the great Allied air-base areas of New Guinea.

Nothing about it was self-sufficient: supplies came overland from the harbour at Oro Bay, and the bay was what fed the field. Station records compiled by Pacific Wrecks place the 90th Bombardment Squadron at Horanda strip, also called Dobodura No. 4, from 21 May 1943, having moved up from Port Moresby, with group headquarters logged the day before; the standard USAAF station list gives the 3rd Bombardment Group at Dobodura from 20 May 1943. The squadron stayed there about eight months, longer than at any other New Guinea station. Allen’s “below the bay” is a fair description of the place: Oro Bay lay to the south-east.

Sources: Pacific Wrecks — Allied units based at Dobodura Airfield; Pacific Wrecks — Dobodura Airfield (Dobodura Airfield Complex), Oro Province, PNG; Army Air Corps Museum — 3rd Bombardment Group (station list after Maurer, USAF Historical Division); Dobodura Airfield Complex — Oro Bay port and road (overview).

“Angel Island, I think they called it”

The depot Allen remembers is Fort McDowell, the Army post on Angel Island’s east garrison, and by 1944 it was part of the San Francisco Port of Embarkation alongside Fort Mason, the Oakland Army Base and Camp Stoneman. Fort McDowell had been the Army’s Overseas Discharge and Replacement Depot since November 1922, and in the war it worked in both directions: it staged more than 300,000 men out to the Pacific, and it took them back in, re-clothing them and straightening their records before loading them on trains east. Men crossed to it on the Army ferry General Frank M.

Coxe, which during the war made as many as eight scheduled runs a day between Fort Mason and Fort McDowell, with periodic stops at Alcatraz. That geography explains the moment of panic in his account — marched off one pier only to find himself alongside another ship, “Oh, my God, they’re going to take us back over there again” — because the transports and the island ferry used the same stretch of waterfront. The island’s mess hall was serving more than 12,000 meals a day; the flag came down at Fort McDowell for the last time on 28 August 1946.

Sources: Historic California Posts: Fort McDowell (California State Military Museum); Ft. McDowell (aka East Garrison) — Angel Island Conservancy; USAT General Frank M. Coxe — Wikipedia; San Francisco Port of Embarkation — Wikipedia.

Prisoners and Losses

Two moments Allen's camera recorded near Hollandia, and the cost of the campaign.

In Memoriam

The 3rd Bomb Group's own history book closes its record of the war with a memorial roll: roughly 350 names of the group's own men who did not come home, prefaced by a short poem signed Edward Fenton — “All that I have I give. Yet all the world's abounding words cannot decrease my wonderment unending, as death, my sole release, buys your salvation: peace.” Allen's own name is not on that list; he is one of the ones who did come home, which is the reason this document exists to tell his story at all.

Source: The Reaper's Harvest, 3rd Attack Group Association.

Documents He Brought Home

The New Guinea field newspaper, a signed occupation note, and Japanese-language leaflets Allen kept from his service.

Psychological Warfare Branch Leaflets

General MacArthur's Southwest Pacific Area Psychological Warfare Branch, formed in Brisbane in June 1944, produced close to 200 different leaflets in its “J1” numbered series — small codes like “25J1” or “159J1” printed directly on the leaflet identified which one it was. The Sixth Army's own Psywar Branch, formed that same September at Hollandia, used a separate “J6” series. No printed code is visible in these particular photographs, so which specific leaflet numbers Allen's are couldn't be confirmed without a clearer scan of the corners and margins where the SWPA numbering was usually stamped.

Sources: psywarrior.com; arsof-history.org.

The mop crew was an official program likely

The stage crew Allen watched may well have been working from a kit. The Army’s Special Services Division ran a formal soldier-show program, issuing complete do-it-yourself packages that contained the script, orchestrations, set and costume designs, choreography and even program templates, so that men at a station could build the scenery, play the instruments and perform for each other. Four of these Blueprint Specials reached the field — About Face!, written by Frank Loesser, Arnold Auerbach and others; Hi, Yank!, built around Sgt. George Baker’s Sad Sack; P.F.C.

Mary Brown; and OK, USA! — and alongside them came the USO-Camp Shows “At Ease” volumes and the Army’s numbered Soldier Shows Folios, of which the surviving collection runs from No. 9 to No. 31, the latest of them dated 1945. A 1944 sketch-writing contest, the joint work of the Writers’ War Board and the Army’s Special Service, produced GI Prize Winning Blackouts, a published collection of short comic scenes about Army life chosen from hundreds submitted worldwide. A “blackout” is precisely the shape of what Allen saw: men, props, a known tune, a substituted lyric, and a fast curtain. No source names the show at Atlantic City, or puts that latrine lyric in any printed script — only the machinery that made such evenings routine.

Sources: Soldier Shows — U.S. Army “Blueprint Specials” and Other Soldier Shows, University of North Texas Libraries; Soldier Shows Collection — UNT Digital Library; The Comedy Propaganda Machine: The Soldier Sketch Writing Contest of World War II — University of Maryland.

Parody was the enlisted man’s own repertoire

The Army tried to give soldiers a songbook. The Army Song Book of 1941 offered sixty-seven patriotic, folk and service numbers and organized sing-alongs to go with them, and the men largely declined; their rule was spontaneous or nothing, and they snubbed the Army’s own song sessions.

What they sang instead were parodies, new words fitted to tunes everyone already carried, and the practice is documented in detail: “Bless ‘Em All” was the song American servicemen most liked to sing and to rewrite, and men set their own verses to “The Battle Hymn of the Republic,” “Down in the Valley,” “Mademoiselle from Armentieres” and “As Time Goes By.” Eric Posselt collected such material in Give Out! in 1943, and postal authorities called it lewd and obscene and banned it from the mail, while the FBI took an interest in “Gee, But I Want to Go Home” before concluding it was good-natured griping about Army food. Paul Fussell, writing later about his own war, described soldiers’ profanity as a licensed way for millions of conscripts to register bitterness and anger they could not otherwise speak; the parodies did the same work with a tune underneath. Allen’s latrine version of “Begin the Beguine” is a specimen of exactly that genre, and one of its mildest and most repeatable.

Sources: World War II Soldiers Loved to Sing — Provided They Got to Sing Their Way — HistoryNet; Blood on the Risers — Wikipedia; Soldiers’ Songs: The Folklore of the Powerless — Buffalo State College.

The song everyone in the room already knew

Cole Porter wrote “Begin the Beguine” on a 1935 cruise aboard the Franconia, between Kalabahi and Fiji, and gave it to the Broadway musical Jubilee, where June Knight introduced it at the Imperial Theatre in October 1935; the show failed, the song did not catch, and the musicologist Alec Wilder later called it “a maverick, it is an unprecedented experiment,” a tune he could not sing or whistle through without the printed music. What made it universal was Artie Shaw. Shaw recorded Jerry Gray’s arrangement at RCA Victor’s Studio 2 in New York on 24 July 1938; the men at RCA thought the idea “a complete waste of time” and put it on the B-side of “Indian Love Call,” the number everyone, Shaw included, expected to sell.

The disc jockeys chose the beguine side instead. It reached number three, made Shaw a national figure, and by the 1960s was reckoned to have sold some six and a half million copies. The Library of Congress essay on the record adds one detail this family will want: Porter’s tune, it says, was inspired by a folk number he had heard in New Guinea. That is the reason the gag Allen describes worked at all — by the autumn of 1944 a stage crew had only to walk out with mops and brooms and hit the first phrase, and every man in the hall supplied the original words in his head while the substituted ones landed on top of them.

Sources: Begin the Beguine — Wikipedia; “Begin the Beguine” — Artie Shaw & His Orchestra (1938), National Recording Preservation Board essay, Library of Congress; Artie Shaw — Wikipedia; Artie Shaw And His Orchestra, Begin The Beguine (1945 jukebox pressing) — Discogs.

“A 21-day delay en route” — and a hotel in Atlantic City

“Delay en route” is not soldier’s slang; it is an Army administrative term for authorised travel time granted between duty stations, governed for enlisted men by the Army’s regulations on furloughs, passes and delays. For Army Air Forces men back from overseas, that leave at home was followed by a redistribution station, and Allen’s was the first one the AAF ever opened. The AAF activated its Redistribution Center at Atlantic City on 15 August 1943, along with Redistribution Station No. 1 there and Station No. 2 at Miami Beach, with the mission “to receive all Army Air Forces Personnel returning to the continental United States from overseas” and then, after examination and re-evaluation, to assign them to appropriate stations, detail them to rest camps or effect their separation from the service.

The hotel he reported to was one of forty-seven Atlantic City hotels the Army had leased at a dollar a day per room; Chalfonte-Haddon Hall and the Traymore had together become Thomas M. England General Hospital, the Traymore holding its convalescent centre with its rehabilitation equipment for amputees. So his two interviews — the one where he named three stations near home, and the one where he was offered Atlantic City itself at the price of two grades — were the “examination and re-evaluation” the directive describes, and the dances, the shows and the mops-and-brooms latrine version of “Begin the Beguine” were part of the design rather than a windfall. At the Santa Monica station the Army set aside a whole hotel for married soldiers, and something like it at Atlantic City is the likeliest reason the honeymoon could simply carry on.

Sources: Craven & Cate, The Army Air Forces in World War II, Vol. VII: Services Around the World, Chapter 17 (HyperWar); “War at the Shore” — Atlantic City Weekly; Atlantic City Training Center — Wikipedia; Camp Boardwalk and Atlantic City Veterans — Atlantic City Free Public Library, Heston Archives.

What two grades were worth likely

Under the Pay Readjustment Act of 1942, effective 1 June 1942, which set the rates for nearly the whole war, a first-grade noncommissioned officer, a master sergeant, drew $138.00 a month in base pay under three years of service and $144.90 with more than three years; two grades below him, in the third grade, a staff sergeant or technician third grade drew $96.00 and $100.80. For a man who had been in federal service since 16 September 1940, and so past the three-year mark, accepting the Atlantic City posting on those terms meant handing back $44.10 a month, a little over thirty percent of his base pay, along with the standing of the top enlisted grade he had reached overseas.

The structural reason such an offer could be made at all is the Table of Organization, the document that “established a unit’s strength by duty position and grade”: when every authorized slot at a grade was filled, no further man could be carried in it, and the making and breaking of noncommissioned officers ran on the Army’s own enlisted-grade regulations rather than on a commander’s goodwill. Allen’s account of DeRidder shows the same squeeze from the other side, a base authorized one master sergeant with five returned master sergeants standing in front of it and a major proposing a school and a competition for the single place. What the record does not settle is whether a formal Army Air Forces policy in 1944 and 1945 directed redistribution stations to seek such reductions — the official history of the redistribution program is silent on grade — or whether it was a local expedient; on that, his sentence is the evidence.

Sources: 1942–1946 Military Pay Chart (Pay Readjustment Act of 1942) — NavyCS; Comparison of military and civilian pay in WWII, Barron’s (reprinted); Assignment & Promotion — The American Soldier in World War II; United States Army enlisted rank insignia of World War II — Wikipedia.

Coffeyville, Kansas, was a real station

The town the tent used to laugh about had an Army airfield seven miles to its northeast, on a 1,456-acre tract where construction began on 1 June 1942; it was activated on 17 June 1942 as an Army Air Forces basic flying school, one of more than a dozen AAF fields Kansas would hold before the war ended. Basic pilot training in BT-13 Valiants opened on 14 November 1942 with Class 43-C, of whose 137 cadets 116 graduated on 13 January 1943, and in sixteen classes some 4,840 cadets and aviation students began the course while 3,881 finished it.

On 1 June 1944 the field passed to Third Air Force, which organized there the Coffeyville Replacement Training Unit (Photo Reconnaissance), redesignated three months later the Coffeyville Combat Crew Training Station (Photo Reconnaissance); the first pilots reported on 12 June 1944, and more than 460 finished their training in the twelve months that followed, first on the F-10, the camera version of the B-25, and then increasingly on the F-5, the unarmed camera version of the P-38. That is the station waiting behind the name on the Atlantic City bulletin board in the autumn of 1944, and its first camera ships were built on the same airframe Allen’s own squadron had flown across New Guinea. A War Department telegram of 2 October 1945 authorized announcing the field’s temporary inactivation, and the deed passed to the city on 21 July 1947; it is the Coffeyville Municipal Airport today.

Sources: Coffeyville Army Air Field — Wikipedia; Kansas World War II army airfields — Wikipedia; Coffeyville Municipal Airport — Wikipedia.

The 369th, and a move he missed by one day

The outfit Allen joined had a short and entirely domestic life. The 369th Fighter Group was constituted on 26 May 1943 and activated at Hamilton Field, California on 1 August 1943; it worked as a fighter Replacement Training Unit through Marysville and Oroville, came back to Hamilton, then moved to DeRidder Army Air Base on 28 March 1944, where it took part in air-ground manoeuvres and demonstrations including the Louisiana Manoeuvres of summer 1944.

It flew P-39 Airacobras, then A-36 Apaches, P-40 Warhawks and finally P-51 Mustangs, and it never went overseas; it was inactivated on 10 August 1945. On 31 January 1945 Stuttgart Army Air Field, Arkansas — built in 1942 under the 70,000 Pilot Training Program, first a glider school and then an advanced twin-engine flying school, with four 5,000-foot runways and seven auxiliary fields — was transferred to Third Air Force and became a replacement training school under the 369th. The group moved there on 8 February 1945, which is the move Allen missed by a single day, lying in the DeRidder hospital with malaria while his wife waited at the hotel in town.

Sources: 369th Fighter Group — Wikipedia; 369th Fighter Group — Army Air Corps Museum; 369th Fighter Group — History of War; Stuttgart Army Air Field (Arkansas) — Wikipedia.

DeRidder: one slot, five master sergeants likely

DeRidder Army Air Base had been built on land leased from the Beauregard Parish Police Jury from 1 July 1941, and by the wet night Allen arrived it was in its last phase: on 31 March 1944 the II Tactical Air Division of III Tactical Air Command was assigned there to conduct replacement training, and training at DeRidder ceased altogether in February 1945. We could not find any published source describing DeRidder as an “air raid warning school,” so that part of his account stands on his word alone — and the command’s own stated mission runs to dive bombardment, light bombardment and reconnaissance training, with no mention of aircraft-warning work, so the record neither backs him nor contradicts him here.

What the record does confirm is the door he talked his way through. The 369th Fighter Group, with its 398th, 399th and 400th Fighter Squadrons, had been stationed at DeRidder since 28 March 1944 — so a major picking up a telephone and finding three openings in a fighter squadron is entirely consistent with what was sitting on that same field. His own explanation of why he refused the competition is worth keeping as he said it: men who had done the work for years should not have to compete against someone given a crash course in it.

Sources: Beauregard Regional Airport (DeRidder Army Air Base) — Wikipedia; 369th Fighter Group — Wikipedia; III Tactical Air Command — Wikipedia; World War II DeRidder Army Air Base Memorial Historical Marker (HMdb).

The 399th Fighter Squadron

The 369th Fighter Group — its 398th, 399th, and 400th Fighter Squadrons — activated August 1, 1943, at Hamilton Field, California, and moved to DeRidder Army Air Base, Louisiana, on March 28, 1944. It was a training group, not a combat unit: through 1944 its pilots flew P-39 Airacobras, A-36s, and P-40s in air-ground maneuvers, including that summer's large-scale Louisiana Maneuvers, before re-equipping with P-51 Mustangs in 1945. The group moved to Stuttgart Army Airfield, Arkansas, on February 8, 1945 — matching Allen's own service record exactly — and was inactivated that August, days after the war's end.

Sources: Air Force Historical Research Agency; Army Air Corps Museum.

“A number of points” — and Fort Dix

The points were the Adjusted Service Rating Score, the War Department’s attempt at an equitable order of discharge, announced on 10 May 1945, two days after the German surrender. A man earned one point for every month of service counted from 16 September 1940, a second point for every month of that service spent overseas, five points for each decoration or campaign participation star, and twelve points for each dependent child up to three; an enlisted man needed eighty-five to be considered for release.

Allen had entered federal service on 16 September 1940, the very day the clock began, had been overseas from January 1942 to the autumn of 1944, and was credited with five campaigns — which on the published rule puts him comfortably above the threshold rather than near it. (That is arithmetic applied to the regulation and his campaign credits, not a figure copied from his papers; the score as actually computed would be in his separation records.) He was discharged at Fort Dix on 8 June 1945, four weeks after the system was announced — a place that would put more than 1.2 million soldiers back into civilian clothes before it was finished with the job. He turned down the reenlistment interview, and got on the train.

Sources: Adjusted Service Rating Score — Wikipedia; Demobilization of United States Armed Forces after World War II — Wikipedia; Fort Dix — GlobalSecurity.org; Fort Dix — Wikipedia.

Three More Attacks, and the One He Refused to Report

The attacks Allen suffered at DeRidder and Stuttgart were not new infections. Plasmodium vivax, the relapsing one of the two New Guinea malarias, leaves dormant parasites in the liver, and neither quinine nor Atabrine could reach them — the drugs suppressed the blood stages only, so relapses typically began about four weeks after a man stopped taking them. Among Allied soldiers with up to a year’s exposure, more than 80 per cent relapsed; in one series of 328 Pacific veterans followed in Minnesota after their suppressive drugs were withdrawn, a quarter of the relapse histories ended within the first year, 53 per cent ran on through the second, and 18 per cent were still going in the third, with a few men relapsing out to four years.

No radical cure existed during the war — primaquine came afterwards — and the Army designated general hospitals in the States as centres for tropical disease, among them Harmon General at Longview, Texas, which also ran a laboratory for imported malaria studies. That is the context for the hardest detail in Part 2: the night before he was to leave for Fort Dix, Allen felt an attack coming and said nothing. The Army had announced its 85-point discharge score on 10 May 1945 and he had the points; a fever reported to the orderly room would have cost him his place in the queue, so he lay down, took the fevers and the chills for an hour and a half, and went to the pictures.

Sources: Plasmodium vivax Relapse Rates in Allied Soldiers during the Second World War: Importance of Hypnozoite Burden, American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene 107(6), 2022; Demobilization of United States Armed Forces after World War II (Adjusted Service Rating Score, announced 10 May 1945, critical score 85); Preventive Medicine in World War II, Vol. VI, Chapter X: Southwest Pacific Area; Harmon General Hospital, Handbook of Texas, Texas State Historical Association.

The Point System

The “number of points” Allen mentions was the Adjusted Service Rating Score, announced May 10, 1945, two days after Germany's surrender: one point per month of service, one more per month served overseas, five points per battle star or decoration, and twelve points per dependent child (to a maximum of three). Eighty-five points was the initial threshold for discharge eligibility, later lowered to as few as fifty as the Pacific War wound down. Troops called it simply “the point system.”

Source: The National WWII Museum, “The Points Were All That Mattered.”
